turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll grab your obs before Dr Lang comes in. Blood pressure's one twenty-eight over seventy-eight, heart rate's one hundred and eight, oxygen sat ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): A hundred and eight? Is that dangerous? I can feel it in my throat just sitting here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): It's on the quick side, but I'm not the one to unpack it. She'll be in in a tick.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr Lang. Racing heart, is that what's brought you in?

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, and I get really puffed, like I can't finish a sentence. It's worse at night in bed, and it also kicks off before exams or if I've got a meeting at work. But I don't think it's stress. I'm not a stressy person.
[SEG0006] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'm his partner, I live with him. It's been three months, easy, since the start of autumn. He bolts upright at night with it.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It is not three months. It's six weeks, maybe a bit over. And I don't bolt upright every night, just some nights.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): So you two don't quite line up on the timing. I'll park it as weeks to a few months. With the racing, any dizziness? Any chest pain?
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He goes pale and dizzy. I've watched him grab the bench and sit down.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not get dizzy. There's no chest pain. It's just this thumping. She's worrying more than I am.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): The breathlessness — with the thumping, or on its own? And when did the puffing actually start?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): With it. I can't get a proper breath in, worse lying down at night. Before meetings too, but that's a stuffy room, not... you know. The start, I can't put a date on it, it just crept up.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): How much coffee are you putting away?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I ask something first? Could this actually be my heart packing up? I'm only twenty-four, but my uncle—
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): His uncle had a heart attack at sixty. Totally different thing. Tell her about the coffee.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, sorry. Six or seven long blacks a day, and most arvos a couple of those big V cans. Sometimes three if I'm cramming.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you vape, or smoke cigarettes?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Vape. Nicotine, the twenty milligram pods, pretty much all day. I was going to quit before the exams but—
[SEG0019] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He gets through a pod every day and a half. And he reckons he's fine, but he's awake revising till two. He doesn't sleep.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep. Well, not properly — the heart thing wakes me, that's all. I am not anxious. Can we not make this a stress thing?
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any tablets just now, prescribed or from the chemist?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I tried something a couple of weeks back for the racing, little brown bottle, white tablets. Never clocked the name. Maybe two a day? Stopped last week, they did nothing.
[SEG0023] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I thought they were magnesium.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): They weren't, I don't think. I honestly couldn't tell you what was in them.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I had amoxicillin last year for a sore throat and I was completely fine.
[SEG0027] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Your mum always said you came up in a swelling with penicillin when you were little.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That story's ancient and I don't buy it. If the amoxicillin was fine, I'm not allergic.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations? Previous heart trouble?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations. Heart was fine until this started.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Sorry we were twenty minutes late, by the way. Parramatta Road was banked up forever.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): That rain this morning didn't help. I got soaked just crossing from the car park.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): We had the cricket on the radio the whole way. Sheffield Shield, Smith was set, and then they stopped for the rain.
[SEG0034] person_4 (CAREGIVER): And that nick they didn't even review. He'll be filthy.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I was yelling at the radio like an idiot. Anyway.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I only caught the highlights. Righto, back to you. Let me have a listen.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pulse is regular, just fast. Heart sounds are normal. Lungs are clear, no wheeze. No swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any weight change, feeling unusually hot, or shaky hands? I'm asking with the thyroid in mind.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): I've dropped a bit of weight, but I've been skipping lunch, so that might be why. I do feel hot at night when it happens. Hands aren't shaky. Is a bit of weight loss a bad sign, and how much is too much?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Without a number I can't call it good or bad. Skipping lunch muddies it, so I won't hang a story on the weight.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do you actually think this is? Am I going to collapse before the exam? Do I have to stop coffee completely? And does an ECG hurt?

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to tell you you're about to collapse. Thinking it through, the coffee, the energy drinks and the vaping can all drive a fast heart and that air hunger, an overactive thyroid can look just the same, and I can't rule out a rhythm problem until we've got a tracing. I am not labelling this anxiety. The timing around exams is a flag, not a diagnosis.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): If the thyroid's normal and the ECG's normal, then what? Do I just live like this? Can I keep vaping if I cut the coffee? What if I faint — I haven't fainted, I'm just asking.

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If those come back normal and the episodes are still happening, we might organise a Holter, a recorder you wear for a day or so. Not ordering that today — let's see what the tests say. I'd like you to wind the coffee and the Vs right down, and have a real go at stopping the vape. I'll also show you a slow breathing exercise for when it starts at night — in for four, out for six, a few minutes.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the breathing instead of coming back? When do I come back? And who rings me if something's wrong on the bloods?

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathing is for the episodes, not instead of review. Come back in a fortnight either way and we'll go through it together; we'll contact you sooner if something on the tests needs it. I'll order an ECG today, plus thyroid bloods, a TSH and a free T4. If you faint, or you get heavy chest pain, don't wait for the fortnight, go to emergency.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you down for the ECG, and the blood form will be at the desk. Won't take long.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: Pod use every day and a half was reported by caregiver, not patient.
bad.text: smoking (description=Vapes nicotine 20 mg pods through the day, about one pod every day and a half, status=current, details=Had been planning to quit before exams, reported_by=patient)

bad.reason: Patient said 'maybe two a day'; exact dose is uncertain, not definitive.
bad.text: unidentified white tablets from a brown bottle (dose=2 tablets, frequency=per day, indication=palpitations, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Breathlessness was described as severe enough that he 'can't finish a sentence' / 'can't get a proper breath in'.
Negative finding: patient denied dizziness ('I do not get dizzy').
Medication detail missing: the unidentified tablets were started 'a couple of weeks back' and stopped last week because they 'did nothing'.
Allergy history nuance missing/wrongly captured: patient specifically reported tolerating amoxicillin last year for a sore throat without any reaction.
History/exam-related symptom detail missing: patient said he can feel the fast heart 'in my throat' even while sitting still.
Negative finding asked and answered: patient had not fainted ('I haven't fainted, I'm just asking').
Assessment/plan detail: doctor explicitly stated she was 'not labelling this anxiety'; exam timing is only a flag, not a diagnosis.

omissions.text: Patient denied bolting upright every night, saying it happens only some nights.
Patient denied that breathlessness occurs on its own; he said it happens with the thumping/racing heart.

Doctor noted lungs were clear with no wheeze and there was no swelling at the ankles; no oedema/ankle swelling is an examination finding already captured, but the explicit absence of wheeze and ankle swelling were stated together as part of the exam.
Patient denied feeling unusually anxious/stressy and specifically asked not to make this a stress thing; this is stronger than simply denying anxiety symptoms.
Patient denied loss of consciousness when asking about what to do if he faints: 'I haven't fainted, I'm just asking.'
Doctor explicitly said Holter monitor was not being ordered today, only to be considered later if tests are normal and episodes continue.
Doctor clarified that the slow breathing exercise is for episodes and is not a substitute for review.
